Gabriel's Horn

Spin a curve into a horn and meet a paradox. The volume is finite but the surface area is infinite.

Filling the inside and painting the outside behave differently. The thinning rate splits the two computations. One total stops growing while the other never does.

For example, a coiled 🧵 string fits inside a small 📦 box. Spread that same string flat across the floor and it would need an endless room.

Resolve the 'painter's paradox': the horn can be filled with π\piπ of paint since its volume is π\piπ, but prove that coating its surface with a uniform coat of thickness δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 needs infinitely much paint.

By problem 2, A(R)→∞A(R) \to \inftyA(R)→∞, so the coating volume diverges to ∞\infty∞ for every δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 — no finite paint coats the whole surface.

  4. Why it is not a paradox: 'filling' spends the volume π\piπ, while 'coating' spends thickness times area — two different quantities.

    One being finite and the other infinite is no contradiction.

    This is exactly where the physical intuition that paint has thickness breaks down.
